content.text: 30th Birthday Party Plan
Vision
A warm, memorable night celebrating a big milestone with her closest friends and family. Aim for a vibe that feels like her: relaxed, fun, and personal rather than over-produced.
Key decisions
Surprise or not? Decide who needs to be in on the secret
Pick the date and time
Choose venue (home, restaurant, rented space, outdoors)
Lock in the theme and dress code
Set the total budget
Theme & vibe
Theme ideas: "Dirty Thirty" cocktail night, garden party, 2000s throwback, dinner party
Colour palette:
Signature drink / cake flavour:
Milestones
6-8 weeks out: book venue, set budget, draft guest list
4-6 weeks out: send invitations, book caterer/bakery
2 weeks out: chase RSVPs, finalise menu, order decor
Week of: confirm vendors, buy drinks, build playlist
Day before: set up, prep food, charge speakers/camera

content.text: 7-Day Prep Plan
Goal: walk into the interview knowing the company, the role, my stories, and the fintech fundamentals cold.
Days 7-6: Research
Re-read the job description and highlight the top 5 requirements
Fill in the Company research page (products, customers, competitors, news)
Look up each interviewer on LinkedIn
Days 5-4: Stories and fundamentals
Write 6 STAR stories covering the common themes
Review payments, lending, KYC/AML and compliance basics
Draft a 60-second "Tell me about yourself"
Days 3-2: Practice
Answer 10 questions from the Question bank out loud, timed
Do a technical or case practice session (coding, SQL, or product case)
Run a mock interview with a friend
Day 1: Logistics and rest
Test the video link, camera, mic, and internet (or plan the route)
Lay out clothes, print resume copies, and prepare questions to ask
Get a full night of sleep

- **Interchange**: fee paid by the merchant's bank to the card issuer on each card transaction

- **PSD2 / SCA**: EU rules requiring strong customer authentication

data.title: Project Brief: Moving the Team Wiki into PlexiiWrite

content.text: Purpose

Our team wiki currently lives in [current wiki tool]. This project moves it into PlexiiWrite so the team works from one place for documentation, with content that is current, easy to find and clearly owned. This brief sets out what we want from the move, what is and is not included, when it happens, and what could go wrong.
Goals
The move should be more than a copy-and-paste. A successful migration means:
Every page the team still relies on is available in PlexiiWrite, with formatting, images and attachments intact.
Outdated or duplicate pages are retired rather than carried over.
Each remaining section has a named owner who keeps it up to date.
The team can find what it needs in PlexiiWrite at least as easily as before.
The old wiki is switched to read-only and then archived, so there is no ambiguity about which one is current.
Scope

In scope are all active pages, attachments and embedded media in the current wiki, the folder or page structure in PlexiiWrite, access permissions for the team, and a short guide to help people get started.

Out of scope are rewriting content beyond what is needed to fix broken formatting, building integrations with other tools, and migrating documents that live outside the wiki, such as files on shared drives. These can be picked up as follow-on work if needed.
Approach and timeline
The work runs in five phases. Dates and owners are to be confirmed.
Audit and cleanup, [start date] to [end date]. Inventory existing pages, mark each as keep, update or retire, and assign section owners.
Structure and setup, [dates]. Design the page hierarchy in PlexiiWrite, set permissions, and agree on simple naming and formatting conventions.
Pilot migration, [dates]. Move one or two sections, check formatting, links and attachments, and note any problems before scaling up.
Full migration, [dates]. Move the remaining approved content, fix broken links, and have owners review their sections.
Cutover and archive, [date]. Announce the switch, set the old wiki to read-only, and archive it after an agreed grace period of [length].
Roles
Project lead: [name], responsible for schedule, decisions and communication.
Section owners: [names], responsible for reviewing and signing off their content.
PlexiiWrite admin: [name], responsible for setup, permissions and troubleshooting.
Risks

Broken links and formatting. Internal links, tables and embedded files often do not survive a move cleanly. The pilot phase is meant to surface this early, and owners will review their sections after migration.
Content bloat. Without a cleanup step, outdated pages move across and the new wiki is just as cluttered as the old one. The audit phase and owner sign-off guard against this.
Permissions errors. Content could end up visible to the wrong people, or hidden from people who need it. Permissions will be checked against the current setup before cutover.
Low adoption. If people keep editing the old wiki, content will split across two places. A clear cutover date, a read-only switch and a short getting-started guide reduce this risk.
Stretched capacity. Owners have day jobs, and review work can slip. Keeping each owner's section small and the deadlines visible helps.
Open questions
What is the target completion date, and is it fixed?
Does anything in the current wiki have retention or compliance requirements before it can be archived or deleted?
Who has final say on what gets retired during the audit?

content.text: Welcome

Welcome to the support team. This guide covers what your first week looks like, the tools you will use, and how we handle escalations. You are not expected to know everything by Friday. The goal of the first week is to get you comfortable with our product, our tools and our people, and to have you handling real customer conversations with support from a teammate.
Your onboarding buddy is [buddy name] and your manager is [manager name]. Ask either of them anything, at any time. Questions in week one are a sign you are paying attention.
What good support looks like here
Before the details, a few principles that shape how we work:
Customers contact us because something is blocking them. Our first job is to understand the problem, not to defend the product.
A clear, honest answer beats a fast, vague one. If you do not know, say so and tell the customer what happens next.
We own a conversation until it is resolved or properly handed to someone else. Handing off does not mean disappearing.
We write like people. Short sentences, plain words, no jargon the customer has not used themselves.
[Add or replace with your team's own values and tone guidelines.]
Your first week
The shape below is a suggested rhythm. Adjust the days and items to match how your team actually runs onboarding.
Day one: orientation and access

Meet your manager and your buddy, and get introduced to the wider team. Confirm you have access to every tool listed in the next section. If anything is missing, tell [person or channel for access requests] right away, since waiting on access is the most common way new starters lose a day.

Spend the rest of the day reading. Start with our help center and internal knowledge base so you see the product the way customers are told about it. Skim our style guide and macros or saved replies so you know how we sound.
Days two and three: learn the product and shadow
Use the product yourself. Set up a test account, work through the main workflows, and try to break things. You will understand customer problems much faster if you have made the same mistakes.

Shadow your buddy on live tickets [and calls or chats, if applicable]. Pay attention to how they read a ticket, what they check first, how they phrase a reply, and when they decide to escalate. Keep a running list of questions and go through it with them at the end of each day.
Day four: handle tickets with a safety net

Start answering real tickets, with your buddy reviewing replies before they are sent. Begin with the simpler, common issue types and work upward. Expect to be slower than the team average. That is normal and nobody is measuring you against it yet.
Day five: review and plan

Sit down with your manager to look at the week. Go through the replies you sent, what went well, and where you got stuck. Together, set goals for your next few weeks, including when you will move to working independently and which topics you want more training on. [Add your team's targets for ramp-up here, if you have them.]
Tools you will use
You will spend most of your time in a small set of tools. Each one has a specific purpose, so it helps to know which to reach for.

The help desk, [help desk tool], is where tickets arrive, are assigned and are answered. Learn the views, tags and statuses your team uses, and how to add internal notes that a colleague could pick up cold.
The knowledge base, [knowledge base location], holds the articles customers see and any internal-only guidance. Search it before you answer anything, and flag articles that are wrong or missing.
Team chat, [chat tool], is for quick questions, live incident updates and coordination. Use [channel name] for support questions and [channel name] for urgent issues.
The bug and feature tracker, [issue tracker], is where engineering issues are logged. Check whether a problem is already reported before creating a new one, and link the ticket to the issue.

Internal admin or account tools, [admin tool], let you look up customer accounts. Only access what you need to solve the customer's problem, and never share account details outside the proper channels.
[Any other tools, such as a phone system, status page or call recording software.]
Working a ticket
A reliable routine will make you faster and more consistent. For each ticket:
Read the whole message and any history before you reply. Check for earlier tickets from the same customer.
Work out what the customer actually needs, which is sometimes different from what they asked.
Search the knowledge base and tracker for a known answer or known issue.
Reproduce the problem when you can. If you cannot, ask for the specific details you need in a single message rather than several.
Reply clearly, say what you did or what happens next, and set an honest expectation about timing.
Tag and categorize the ticket correctly so our reporting stays useful.
Our response and resolution targets are [response time target] for first reply and [resolution target] for resolution. [Confirm whether targets vary by plan, channel or priority.]
How we handle escalations
Escalation is a normal part of the job, not a failure. The aim is to get the customer to the person best placed to fix the problem, with everything that person needs to act quickly.
When to escalate
Escalate when any of the following applies:
The issue appears to be a bug, outage or data problem that support cannot fix.
The request is outside what you are authorized to do, such as [examples: refunds above a limit, account exceptions, policy changes].
The customer is at risk of serious harm or loss, including security concerns, billing errors with significant impact, or legal and compliance questions.
The customer is very frustrated, has been waiting a long time, or has asked for a manager.
You have worked the problem properly and are still stuck.
If you are unsure, ask your buddy or lead before escalating. Over time you will build a feel for the line.
Escalation levels and routes
[Describe your actual structure here. A typical shape is below; replace it with yours.]
For general questions and second opinions, ask in [channel name] or tag your buddy.
For product defects, escalate to [engineering contact or process] through [issue tracker], using the priority definitions in [link to priority guide].
For billing and account exceptions, go to [billing or finance contact].

For security, privacy or legal matters, go straight to [security or legal contact] and tell your lead. Do not continue the conversation with the customer beyond a holding reply until you have guidance.
For urgent or high-impact incidents, use [on-call or incident process] and notify [manager name].
What a good escalation contains
Whoever picks up your escalation should not have to go back to the customer to ask basic questions. Include:
A one-line summary of the problem and its impact.
The customer's account or ID and their plan, if relevant.
Steps to reproduce, or exactly what you tried and what happened.
Screenshots, logs or error messages.
Links to related tickets or known issues.
What you have already told the customer, and what you have promised.
The deadline or urgency, and why.
After you escalate

Tell the customer that you have passed the issue on, who is looking at it and when they can expect an update, even if the update is that there is no news yet. Stay on the ticket. Check back at the interval you promised, keep notes current, and close the loop with the customer once the issue is resolved. If an escalation has stalled, follow up with the owner and tell your lead rather than letting it sit.
Your first few weeks

Over the following weeks you will take on more volume and more complex issue types, and your buddy's review will taper off as you show consistency. You will also join [recurring team meetings, such as weekly team sync or quality reviews]. Quality reviews are meant to help you improve and are not a test.

We also want your fresh perspective. If you notice a confusing article, a repetitive question that could be prevented, or a process that feels clumsy, say so. New eyes catch things the rest of us have stopped seeing.
Useful contacts
Manager: [manager name and contact]
Onboarding buddy: [buddy name and contact]
Access and IT requests: [contact or channel]
HR and people questions: [contact]
Escalation and on-call details: [link or contact]
Checklist for the end of week one
You have access to all the tools above.
You have read the help center and key internal guidance.
You have used the product and completed the main workflows yourself.
You have shadowed at least a few live tickets

slides.title: How to Write a Good Bug Report
slides.notes: Welcome everyone. Over the next few minutes we will cover what makes a bug report useful, what to include, and how to avoid the mistakes that slow fixes down.

slides.title: Why the quality of a report matters
bullets: A clear report saves the engineer from guessing
Vague reports lead to back-and-forth questions
Unreproducible bugs often get closed or ignored
Good reports get fixed faster and with fewer mistakes
The report is often the only evidence the bug ever existed
slides.notes: Start with the stakes. The person reading your report usually cannot see your screen or your machine, so everything they know comes from your words. A report that needs three rounds of questions costs everyone time, and the bug waits while it happens.

slides.title: Start with a title that says what broke
bullets: Name the problem, not the feeling, such as 'Export button does nothing on the Reports page'
Mention where it happens and what goes wrong
Keep it to one line someone can scan in a list
Avoid titles like 'Broken' or 'Help, urgent'
One bug per report
slides.notes: The title is what people see in a queue, so it has to carry real information. Compare 'Export is broken' with a title that names the page and the symptom. Also stress one bug per report, because bundled issues are hard to assign and hard to close.

slides.title: The core of the report
bullets: Steps to reproduce, numbered and in order
What you expected to happen
What actually happened
Environment: browser or device, version, account type
How often it happens: every time, sometimes, once
slides.notes: This is the heart of the deck. Write the steps as if the reader has never used the feature, and be specific about what you clicked and typed. Always separate expected from actual, because what feels obviously wrong to you may be a design choice to someone else.

slides.title: Add evidence that saves time
bullets: Screenshot or short screen recording
Exact error message, copied as text
Console logs or relevant log lines if you can get them
Links to related tickets or recent changes
Note anything you already tried, such as a refresh or a different browser
slides.notes: Evidence turns a claim into something an engineer can check. Copy error messages rather than paraphrasing them, since the exact wording is often searchable in the code. If you narrowed the problem down, say how, because that is a head start for whoever picks it up.

slides.title: Before you hit submit
bullets: Try the steps again yourself and confirm they reproduce it
Search for an existing report of the same bug
Check the title and steps read clearly to a stranger
Say how severe it is and who is affected, based on what you know
Stay available to answer follow-up questions
slides.notes: Close with a quick checklist people can use every time. A thirty-second duplicate search and a second run through the steps catch most weak reports. Finish by reminding everyone that a good report is a small act of respect for the person who has to fix it.

Refund Policy FAQ

Can I get a refund?

Yes. If you ask for a refund within 30 days of your purchase, we will refund you in full. After 30 days, we do not offer refunds.

What happens if I cancel after 30 days?

Your cancellation takes effect and you will not be charged again, but we cannot refund payments that are more than 30 days old. The one exception is annual plans, covered below.

How do refunds work for annual plans?

Annual plans are refunded pro rata. That means you get back the portion of your payment that covers the time you have not used, and we keep the portion that covers the time you have. For example, if you cancel halfway through your year, you would receive roughly half of the annual fee back.
